items.title: Henry Johnson interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995
items.q: looking at a transcribed solo, one of Dizzy’s solos

ctx.x: Yeah. Yeah, I think because if you don’t everything ends up sounding like an exercise. You have to breathe life into the phrase by actually putting air into it and breathing with it. And that’s what a lot of the guys that are coming out of schools now, they don’t realize, they work with a lot of transcribed solos. But when you look at a solo on a piece of paper without actually listening to it being done, you don’t really correlate why a guy did this, you know? You see a weird note on there and you think oh,…

You know I was trans — not transcribing but looking at a transcribed solo, one of Dizzy’s solos. And I was looking at the chord changes, and then I was looking at the notes. And I said there are so many wrong notes on there. I said there’s more wrong notes than there is right notes. If you look at it stagnantly on paper, there’s a ton of wrong notes. But if you listen to it at speed it’s exciting because he can play with such authority, that he can take all them wrong notes and sell them to you.
Well see the thing is, there is no wrong note if it’s followed by a right one.
